Balm of Gilead
BAHM of GIL-ee-ud
n. phrase
Balm: an aromatic resin used for healing wounds; Hebrew tsorī (an unidentified aromatic substance from balsam-trees or related). Gilead: the mountainous region east of the Jordan, famous in OT times for its balsam-resin trade. The Balm of Gilead becomes a famous biblical-prophetic image for healing.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Balm of Gilead is an aromatic resin from the balsam-trees of the mountainous Gilead region east of the Jordan, used in OT times for the healing of wounds and as a valuable trade commodity. The substance itself was widely-known and traded across the ancient Near East. Joseph was sold by his brothers to Ishmaelite merchants with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt (Gen 37:25). Jacob sent gifts of a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds to the Egyptian governor (Joseph, unrecognized) as part of his second-journey supplies (Gen 43:11). Ezekiel describes the Phoenician trade-network: Judah, and the land of Israel, they were thy merchants: they traded in thy market wheat of Minnith, and Pannag, and honey, and oil, and balm (Ezek 27:17). The Balm of Gilead was therefore a significant economic and medical product of OT Israel. The supreme biblical use, however, is the prophetic-lament use in Jeremiah 8:22: is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered? The prophet Jeremiah laments the spiritual condition of his people: the wound of their sin is grievous, the disease deep, the suffering severe—and yet they refuse the healing the LORD has provided. The Balm of Gilead, the famous healing substance produced in their own land, is here used as the figure of the healing-grace the LORD has offered: it is available, it is sufficient, it is at hand—but the people refuse it, and so their wound continues unrecovered. The pastoral application across the centuries has been direct. Christ Himself is the Great Physician (Matt 9:12; Mark 2:17; Luke 5:31); His blood is the substantive Balm of Gilead by which the deepest wound of the soul is healed; the gospel announces the healing freely available to every soul that will receive it; the persistence of unrecovered spiritual sickness in any age is not for lack of the Balm but for the refusal to receive it. Jeremiah’s rhetorical question becomes, in the Christian preacher’s mouth, the standing pastoral inquiry: is there no balm in Gilead? Yes, there is; Christ Himself is the Balm; why then is not the health of the soul recovered? The answer is in the soul’s response, not in any deficiency of the Healer or His provision.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BALM as the sap or juice of certain plants, particularly of trees of the genus Balsamodendron; in scripture, the famous Balm of Gilead, an aromatic healing resin from the mountainous region east of the Jordan, used famously in Jeremiah’s lament (Jer 8:22) as the figure of the LORD’s available-but-refused healing for the deep wound of His people’s sin.

BALM, n. — 1. The sap or juice of certain plants, particularly of trees of the genus Balsamodendron, used for medicinal and aromatic purposes. 2. In scripture, the famous Balm of Gilead (Jer 8:22), figuring the healing-grace the LORD provides for the deep wound of His people’s sin.

GILEAD, n. — A mountainous region east of the Jordan, famous in OT times for its balsam-resin trade; biblically significant as the source of the Balm of Gilead, the figure of healing-grace in Jeremiah’s lament.

📖 Key Scripture

Jeremiah 8:22 — "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?"

Genesis 37:25 — "And they sat down to eat bread: and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a company of Ishmeelites came from Gilead with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt."

Jeremiah 46:11 — "Go up into Gilead, and take balm, O virgin, the daughter of Egypt: in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured."

Luke 5:31-32 — "And Jesus answering said unto them, They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Balm-of-Gilead doctrine is corrupted chiefly by sentimentalization that has reduced Jeremiah’s prophetic lament to a comfort-song without the substantive indictment-and-call-to-repentance the prophet’s rhetorical question actually carries—and by the loss of the typological connection to Christ as the Great Physician whose blood is the substantive Balm now offered universally in the gospel.

expand to see more

The sentimentalization of Jeremiah 8:22 in popular Christian usage has reduced the verse to a comfort-song or a soft devotional refrain (there is a balm in Gilead to heal the sin-sick soul, the spiritual’s rendering) without the substantive indictment-and-call-to-repentance the prophet’s rhetorical question actually carries. Jeremiah’s point in context is not that the healing is available (though it is) but that the people are not being healed because they refuse the available healing: why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered? The verse is a lament, not a comfort-song; an indictment, not a soft consolation. The healing is there; the refusal is the people’s. The recovery is the recovery of the prophetic substance: the Balm is real, the Healer is at hand, the offer is genuine—but the soul that refuses the healing continues unrecovered, and the prophetic lament is over the refusal, not over the unavailability.

The deeper substance is the Christological connection. Christ Himself is the Great Physician (Matt 9:12; Mark 2:17; Luke 5:31); His blood is the substantive Balm of Gilead by which the deepest wound of the soul is healed; the gospel announces the healing freely available to every soul that will receive it. To read Jeremiah 8:22 with Christological substance is to hear the prophetic lament as having a contemporary application: the gospel is preached, the Balm is offered, the Great Physician stands ready—and the persistence of unrecovered spiritual sickness in any age, in any soul, is not for lack of the Balm but for the refusal to receive it. The pastoral application is direct: receive the Balm; come to the Great Physician; let the healing be applied to the actual wound of your sin. The recovery of the Christological reading restores both the prophetic seriousness of the lament and the gospel-substance of the answer the lament implicitly demands.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsorī (an unidentified aromatic healing resin); Gileád (the mountainous region east of the Jordan, famous for its balsam-trade); the substance of OT economic-and-medical use becomes the prophetic-Jeremianic figure (Jer 8:22) for the LORD’s healing-grace, typologically fulfilled in Christ as the Great Physician whose blood is the substantive Balm now offered universally in the gospel.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsorī (H6875) — an aromatic resin, possibly from balsam-trees (6 OT uses).

Hebrew Gileád (H1568) — the mountainous trans-Jordan region (over 100 OT uses).

Greek iatros (G2395) — physician (Matt 9:12; Mark 2:17; Luke 4:23; 5:31; Col 4:14 of Luke the beloved physician).

Greek therapeuō (G2323) — to heal (the NT verb of Christ’s healings, with the same root as therapy).

"Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?—Jeremiah’s rhetorical lament over the people’s refusal of available healing."

"Christ is the Great Physician (Matt 9:12); His blood is the substantive Balm by which the deepest wound of the soul is healed; the gospel announces the healing freely available."

"Sentimentalization reduces the prophet’s lament to a comfort-song; recovery of the substance restores both the indictment (the refusal is the people’s) and the gospel-answer (Christ is the Balm now offered)."
